name: Mercy Corps (Prosper Global): all programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Mercy Corps' programme spending and grants by region from its US entity's Form 990 Schedule F, fiscal 2025 (Sub-Saharan Africa 52%, the Middle East and North Africa 15%, Russia and neighbouring states 11%, South America 9%, South Asia 5%, East Asia and the Pacific 4%, Central America and the Caribbean 3%), each region split equally over Mercy Corps' main programme countries there (a judgment: no country split is published).
summary: Mercy Corps (renamed Prosper Global in 2026) spent $509 million on programmes in its year to June 2025, half of it in Sub-Saharan Africa: livelihoods and market systems ($207M), emergency relief ($138M, mostly cash, water and supplies through partners in Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine and elsewhere), peace, governance and education ($90M), health and nutrition ($43M) and recovery ($31M). It counts people reached (over 36 million) but publishes no controlled measure of what its spending achieved, so every branch is built from its spending, its reach or a judged cost per person and the research on that kind of work, and every branch is discounted for missing data. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range {{range}}: the result is mostly uncertainty): half from livelihoods (small consumption gains spread over the 19 million people its economic programmes reach), a third from relief (cash and goods, and a few excess crisis deaths averted), little from water, nutrition, education and peace work. The biggest uncertainties are how much the livelihood programmes raise consumption for the many people they reach only indirectly, the missing-data discount, and crisis-affected people's consumption.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Cost of the programmes, including overhead
Relief spending per person reached
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' counts don't match the relief line: its Form 990 says relief reached '37.6 million people across programs' (Part III line 4b), the same as its organisation-wide total, and its food-security (19 million) and water-security (10 million) counts span the relief, recovery and health lines (Mercy Corps Europe's report, pp. 24, 29); its US entity paid $34.1M of cash grants to about a million people (Schedule F Part III). Anchors: across all its work it reached over 36 million people (p. 14) on $509M of programmes, $14 a person; a month of multipurpose cash in Ukraine or Sudan costs far more per person, emergency water and hygiene supplies in Gaza or Darfur much less. Judgment $25 ($10-60).

People reached by economic-opportunity programmes

source.title: Mercy Corps Europe, Annual Report and Financial Statements FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025; trustees' report on Mercy Corps' global results)
source.quote: These interventions reached over 19 million people across 38 countries.

rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' own count from its organisational outcome measurement for the year to June 2025: everyone its economic-opportunity programmes reached, many through banks, firms, mobile money and radio rather than directly. 38% of its programmes count towards two or more outcome areas (p. 22), so this overlaps the other outcome areas (taken out by the reach share below). It counts participants (Mercy Corps calls these figures 'participant reach', p. 22), not their household members. With overhead, about $13 a person.

rows.label: Share of the civil-society-and-education line spent on education and youth skills
rows.explainer: The line joins peace and good governance with education; Mercy Corps' outcome areas have no education goal (p. 22: economic opportunities, food security, peace and good governance, water security), so education is the smaller part: youth secondary and vocational schooling in Somalia and Nigeria. Judgment 20% (5-40%).

rows.label: Share of the economic-opportunity reach that the livelihood line's spending reaches
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' outcome-area counts overlap and cross its accounting lines: 38% of its programmes count towards two or more outcome areas (Mercy Corps Europe's report, p. 22), and the four areas' 56 million (19 + 19 + 8 + 10 million, pp. 24-29) compare with 36 million people reached (p. 14). Recovery grants, seeds and livestock (valued in the recovery branch) count as economic opportunity too. Judgment 75% (50-95%).

rows.label: Share of the peace and good governance reach that the civil-society line's spending reaches
rows.explainer: The same overlap: peace work is often layered on relief and livelihood programmes (38% of programmes count towards two or more outcome areas, p. 22), so part of the 8 million are reached by programmes booked in other lines. Judgment 75% (50-95%), as for livelihoods.

source.title: Mercy Corps Europe, Annual Report and Financial Statements FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025; trustees' report on Mercy Corps' global results)
source.quote: These interventions reached over 8 million people across 30 countries.

rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' own count for the year to June 2025, from its organisational outcome measurement, in the trustees' report published in March 2026. Its Form 990 for the same year says over 14 million (Part III line 4c), the range's top; the best stays at the outcome measurement's figure, the same source as the other reach counts here. Most are reached thinly: dialogues, radio, local governance work for a whole district.

rows.label: Cost per young person reached by education and skills a year
rows.explainer: Secondary and vocational schooling, teacher training and youth clubs for older youth in fragile places cost more than a primary reading programme (tens of dollars a child; GPE's accelerated grants about $130 for an out-of-school child). Judgment $150 ($50-400).

rows.explainer: Mercy Corps describes the line as water and food security (Form 990 Schedule O), its water-security programmes reaching about 8 million people and food security about 17 million there; the rest is nutrition and child health. Judgment 40% (20-60%).

rows.explainer: Rehabilitated boreholes and water networks, latrines and hygiene promotion in fragile places: rural boreholes cost $15-40 a person served, piped schemes and repaired urban networks more, new supplies with sanitation over $100; Mercy Corps repairs more than it builds. Judgment $80 ($30-200).

rows.explainer: Spending over the judged cost per person.

rows.explainer: Nutrition sites that screen every child, give supplements and refer severe cases, with counselling for mothers and support to clinics: much of the treatment itself (therapeutic food from UNICEF, government staff) is paid by others. Anchors: treating one severely malnourished child costs $150-200, and screening and supplements for every child in an area a few dollars a child; most children reached get only the latter. Judgment $40 ($15-120).

rows.label: Survey-scale consumption per person, Ukraine, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: National-accounts household consumption per person times the site's survey-to-national-accounts ratio for Ukraine.

rows.label: Stand-in consumption for Africa and Asia
rows.explainer: Four East and Southern African countries with recent surveys stand in for Mercy Corps' African and Asian programme countries (Nigeria, Ethiopia, Somalia, Sudan, the DRC, Niger, Mali, Afghanistan), whose own surveys are old or missing.

rows.label: Stand-in consumption for Latin America
rows.explainer: Honduras and Peru stand in for Guatemala, Haiti, Colombia and Venezuela; Haiti, poorer, is a small part of the region's spending (most is in Colombia and Venezuela), and crisis-affected people's lower consumption is in the share below.

rows.label: Average survey consumption per person in Mercy Corps' regions, weighted by spending
rows.formula: ((sf_ssa + sf_asia) * cons_africa_asia + sf_mena * cons_egy + sf_eurasia * cons_ukr + sf_lac * cons_lac) / sf_total
rows.explainer: Each region's stand-in (Egypt for the Middle East) weighted by Schedule F's spending and grants: about $1,000 a year, before the poorer-than-average adjustments below.

rows.label: Crisis-affected people's consumption as a share of their region's average
rows.explainer: People displaced or cut off in Sudan, Gaza, Darfur, eastern DRC or front-line Ukraine consume far less than their region's survey mean; the poorest fifth in these surveys consume about 40% of the mean, and Gaza's and Sudan's economies have collapsed. The Middle East and Ukraine stand-ins start higher, so a little above the poorest fifth: judgment 45% (30-70%).

rows.label: Consumption per person per year of the people relief and recovery reach
rows.explainer: In 2024 US$ at market prices, the same basis as the value delivered, so no PPP factor is needed.

rows.label: Death rate among the people reached during the crisis, without the response
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' relief goes to war zones and disasters: Sudan and Darfur, Gaza, eastern DRC, Somalia, Syria, Haiti, front-line Ukraine. Mortality surveys in African and Middle Eastern crises commonly find crude death rates of 0.3-1 per 10,000 a day (0.011-0.037 a year); Ukraine's and the Caribbean's excess is small, and less of the relief is famine response. Judgment 0.015 (0.01-0.03).

rows.label: Death rate in the same population before the crisis
rows.explainer: The site's crude death rates for three of the largest crisis countries (UN World Population Prospects), so only excess deaths count.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths the response averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: Cash, water and hygiene supplies prevent some deaths from hunger and the infections that follow when water fails, but most people reached are not at risk of dying in the weeks covered. The evidence is weak: the Cochrane review of cash in disasters (Pega et al. 2015) found one drought study with fewer child deaths, very low certainty; long-running cash programmes cut under-five deaths by about 8% (Richterman et al. 2023). Judgment 8% (2-20%): cash in middle-income disasters averts less, food in famine-risk settings more.

rows.label: Relief spending per person-year of crisis covered
rows.explainer: What it costs to cover one person for a year: a month of multipurpose cash in Sudan or Ukraine is $10-15 a person (a household transfer shared by its members), about $150 a year, plus water and hygiene supplies; water trucking and hygiene kits alone cost much less. Judgment $170 ($60-500) a person-year, so that a lower cost per person reached means shorter cover, not more deaths averted.

rows.label: Years of the crisis the response covers per person
rows.explainer: Spending per person reached over spending per person-year: about {{row:years_exposed}} years (two months) at the defaults.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached by relief (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the time covered, times the share the response averts.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Crisis deaths are mostly from diarrhoea, malnutrition and infections: the site's WHO-based age split for diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (facts/death_ages.json).

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The same split, band by band.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The same split; the rest at 50 and over.

rows.label: Value of a death averted by relief (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached by relief, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Diarrhoea and cholera cases averted by emergency water and hygiene: about one episode a year per person in a camp, a fifth averted over the 0.15 years covered, at the GBD weight for moderate diarrhoea (0.188) for about five days, is under 0.0001 DALYs; malnourished children's illness adds some. Judgment 0.0002 (0-0.001), small next to the deaths and goods.

rows.label: Share of the relief cost reaching people as cash, water or goods
rows.explainer: The rest is staff, transport, security and monitoring. Anchor: the Cash Consortium of Sudan, which Mercy Corps leads, spent 'on average £0.60 for each £1 delivered' (Mercy Corps Europe's report, p. 24), so £1 of £1.60 reached people (62%). Judgment 62% (50-80%).

rows.label: Cash, water and goods delivered per person in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: Valued at what it cost to deliver, which for cash is what people get.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person reached by relief
rows.explainer: The cash and goods on the site's one log-income scale over the time they are used: they raise consumption during the months each person is covered (years_exposed), so the gain is years_exposed × ln(1 + value ÷ the consumption of that period), the site's rule for a transfer used within a year.

rows.label: Share of the recovery cost reaching people as grants, seeds, livestock or repairs
rows.explainer: Recovery programmes carry more training and technical staff than cash relief. Judgment 55% (40-75%), below relief's 62%.

rows.label: Recovery goods and grants per person (US$)
Share of recovery grants invested in farms, animals or businesses
rows.explainer: Recovery grants and seeds are meant to be invested; recipients of large unconditional cash transfers in Kenya invested about 40% of them in assets (Haushofer and Shapiro 2016). Judgment 40% (20-60%).

rows.label: Yearly return on the invested part
rows.explainer: GiveWell's analysis of unconditional cash transfers uses about 10% a year on invested transfers; seeds planted in time return a harvest, livestock die in droughts. Judgment 10% (5-20%).

rows.label: Years the invested part keeps paying
rows.explainer: Seeds and tools a season or two, livestock and repaired water points longer, in places where crises recur. Judgment 5 years (2-10).

rows.label: Share of the invested part still there when its returns end
rows.explainer: GiveWell's analysis of unconditional cash transfers counts part of the invested principal as consumed at the end; livestock and tools depreciate, and recurring droughts and fighting destroy assets. Judgment 30% (0-60%).

rows.label: Years over which the consumed part of a recovery grant is spent
rows.explainer: Recovery cash and vouchers tide a household over until a harvest or until a business restarts. The reference class is humanitarian cash for basic needs, paid over a few months: Ukraine's multipurpose cash, for instance, came in three monthly instalments (Disasters Emergency Committee and LSE, Multipurpose Cash Assistance in Ukraine, 2023, p. 19); GiveWell's analysis of unconditional cash transfers, the upper end, counts the consumed part as spent within the first year. Mercy Corps' recovery grants are timed to a planting season or a restart, so a little longer than relief cash: judgment half a year (a quarter to a full year).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person reached by recovery, discounted
rows.formula: rec_consumption_years * ln(1 + rec_value_per_person * (1 - rec_invested_share) / (baseline_consumption * rec_consumption_years)) + ln(1 + rec_value_per_person * rec_invested_share * rec_return_rate / baseline_consumption) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, rec_return_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - 1) + ln(1 + rec_value_per_person * rec_invested_share * rec_principal_recovered / baseline_consumption) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - rec_return_years)
rows.explainer: The consumed part over the months it is spent (the site's rule for a transfer used within a year: t × ln(1 + value ÷ the consumption of those months)), then the invested part's yearly return for its years, starting a year later, and what is left of the principal consumed at the end, all discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Deaths averted by higher incomes, as a share of the consumption benefits
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/aid_value.json), times your value of a life, for the recovery and livelihood branches.

rows.label: Share of the people reached who take part directly (training, grants, savings groups)
rows.explainer: Market-systems programmes count everyone reached through the firms, banks, mobile-money agents and radio shows they work with; direct participants are a minority. At $13 a person reached the programmes can't be working directly with most of them. Judgment 20% (10-40%).

rows.label: Consumption gain for a direct participant
rows.explainer: Graduation programmes raise consumption 5-10% for years at $1,000 or more a household (Banerjee et al. 2015); savings groups find small or no gains (Beaman et al. 2014 Mali; Ksoll et al. 2016 Malawi); farm-input and extension support a few percent. Mercy Corps reports that 50% of people 'impacted' gained new or better jobs (Mercy Corps Europe's report, p. 25), uncontrolled. Judgment 3% (0.5-8%).

rows.label: Gain of a person reached indirectly, as a share of a direct participant's
rows.explainer: Someone who opens a mobile-money account or buys from a supported input dealer gains much less than a trained farmer; few market-systems evaluations isolate it. Judgment 10% (0-30%).

rows.label: People per household where the livelihood programmes run
rows.explainer: The site's household sizes for three of Mercy Corps' larger African programme countries.

rows.label: Share of direct participants counted without their household members
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' published counts appear to be mostly of whole households: cash reach is given in individuals (the Sudan consortium's '1.9M individuals' reached by multipurpose cash, Mercy Corps Europe's report p. 24, a relief programme) and livelihood results in households (Georgia's ALCP: '9,169 rural households' increasing their income, p. 26); the report doesn't say how households are turned into people in the 19 million total. Programmes that count only the person trained or funded (savings-group members, youth skills, small-business grants) are the minority of the livelihood line. Judgment a fifth (0-60%): at 0 every count already includes the household; the high end if most of the 19 million are trainees and members counted alone. This is why the multiplier is near 1.7, not the full household size applied to counts of households.

rows.label: People whose consumption rises per direct participant counted
rows.explainer: Direct participants counted alone share the gain with their households (the shared household size); those counted with their households already are: about 1.7 at the defaults.

rows.label: Years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure for livelihood programmes abroad (@relief_development.livelihood_gain_years, 2 years, 1-4): farming practices and accounts may stick, but most programme gains fade without support; its high end allows for Mercy Corps' climate-resilience work (rangelands restored, drought-tolerant farming).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person reached by livelihoods, discounted
rows.formula: (liv_direct_share * liv_household_gain_multiplier * ln(1 + liv_direct_gain) + (1 - liv_direct_share) * ln(1 + liv_direct_gain * liv_indirect_gain_ratio)) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, liv_years)
rows.explainer: Direct participants' gains (shared with their households) and indirect participants' gains for each year they last, discounted.

rows.label: Conflict deaths per person-year in the communities the peace work reaches
rows.explainer: ACLED recorded 4,482 political-violence deaths in Somalia in 2024 (about 0.00024 per person) and 6,389 militant-Islamist deaths in Burkina Faso (0.00028); Mercy Corps' peace work is in such places (Nigeria's Middle Belt, Mali, Niger, Somalia, the Central African Republic, Iraq) but also in calmer ones (Kenya, Uganda, Guatemala, Indonesia). Judgment 0.00015 (0.00005-0.0004).

rows.label: Share of conflict deaths the peace work averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: A UN and civil-society campaign teaching dispute resolution in Liberian towns resolved more land disputes and reduced violence a year on (Blattman, Hartman and Blair 2014, a randomised trial); Mercy Corps' own trial of vocational training in Afghanistan found no change in support for armed groups (Lyall, Zhou and Imai 2020); its Mali programme reports 94% feeling safe against 58% at baseline, uncontrolled (Mercy Corps Europe's report, p. 29). Most of the 8 million are reached thinly. Judgment 2% (0-8%).

rows.label: Conflict deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: A year's deaths averted: the programmes' yearly flow of people reached against a year's spending.

rows.label: Value of a conflict death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Conflict deaths are mostly of young men: the site's value for a death at 15 to 49, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Consumption gain from less violence, per person reached
rows.explainer: Fewer raids and resolved land disputes let farmers plant and herders and traders move; conflict costs households several percent of consumption where it is active, and the work removes a small share. Judgment 0.2% (0-1%) for a year.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person reached by peace work
Learning gain per young person reached (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Secondary and vocational schooling in Somalia and Nigeria; trials of education programmes in poor countries find a median near 0.1 SD (Evans & Yuan 2022), smaller for older youth and skills training. Judgment 0.08 SD (0.02-0.2).

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of skill still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic: 20%, 10% to 30%), from the Center for Global Development's review of the studies linking adults' reading and maths to their earnings, per SD of skill still there in adult life.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain that lasts into adulthood
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood: {{row:edu_persistence}}, 20% to 70%): test-score gains fade, a fifth to a half of a year's learning carrying into the next grade in Pakistan's schools (Andrabi and others 2011).

rows.label: Years until the young people reached start working
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' education work is with adolescents and youth, closer to work than primary pupils (about 10 years: @education.years_primary_programme_to_work). Judgment 5 years (2-10).

rows.label: Years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: GiveWell's house figure for long-term income gains.

rows.label: Household sharing of the earnings gain
rows.explainer: GiveWell's house figure.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per young person reached, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + edu_learning_gain_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd * edu_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - edu_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × persistence) for each working year, discounted, after the wait to work, shared with the household.

rows.label: Deaths per child-year under five where the health work runs
rows.explainer: Under-five mortality of 80-115 per 1,000 births in Nigeria, Niger, Somalia and Sudan (UN IGME) is about 0.016-0.023 deaths per child-year; higher in Darfur's camps, lower in Kenya. Judgment 0.016 (0.01-0.025).

rows.label: Share of child deaths the health and nutrition work averts among children covered
rows.explainer: Treating severe acute malnutrition averts many deaths among the few children treated; screening, supplements and counselling for every child in an area much less; programme evaluations of community child health at scale mostly found no detectable fall in mortality (Amouzou et al. 2016, Malawi). Judgment 4% (1-10%).

rows.label: Child deaths averted per child covered (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: A year's deaths averted per child covered.

rows.label: Value of a child death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's value of an under-five death, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: The shared figure for health programmes abroad (@relief_development.health_programme_illness_value_ratio, {{row:hlt_morbidity_value_ratio}}, 0-30%): wasting and stunting averted and fewer sick days, beside the deaths.

rows.label: Diarrhoeal deaths per person-year, Sub-Saharan Africa (all ages)
rows.explainer: The rate a water supply acts on, Sub-Saharan Africa's (@sub_saharan_africa.diarrhoea_deaths_per_person_2021, GBD 2021, about 50 per 100,000, 30-80); wide because the estimate varies by country and year.

rows.label: Fall in diarrhoeal deaths from a new or repaired water supply with hygiene work
rows.explainer: Meta-analyses of water interventions (Wolf et al. 2022, Lancet) find large falls in diarrhoea for piped water and chlorination but small, uncertain ones for improved community sources; chlorination trials cut child deaths more (Kremer et al. 2023). Mercy Corps' work is mostly community sources: judgment 12% (0-30%).

rows.label: Other deaths averted per diarrhoeal death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared ratio for water treatment: deaths from other causes that diarrhoea makes more likely.

rows.label: Years a new or repaired water supply serves
rows.explainer: Hand pumps and boreholes last 10-15 years with repairs; repairs in conflict areas and emergency networks fewer. Judgment 8 years (3-15).

rows.label: Share of those years the water supply works
rows.explainer: About a quarter to a third of rural hand pumps in Sub-Saharan Africa are broken at any time (Rural Water Supply Network). Judgment 70% (50-85%).

rows.label: Working years of the water supply, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year's benefit at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Value of a diarrhoeal death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's age split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa by the site's values by age, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person given water (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Diarrhoeal deaths averted, with the other deaths they bring, over the supply's working years, discounted.

rows.label: Value of water-fetching time saved, as a share of consumption
rows.explainer: The shared figure for time saved fetching water, mostly women's and girls' (@water.time_saved_consumption_share, {{row:wash_time_saved_share}} of consumption, 0-3%).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from time saved, over the supply's life
rows.explainer: The time saved on the site's log-income scale for each working year, discounted.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, relief
rows.explainer: Cash and water in crises do what they say (people get the transfer, as cash-transfer evaluations find); the doubt is in the share of deaths averted, already judged low. 0.85 (0.7-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, relief
rows.explainer: Whether the people reached would have been helped anyway. UN humanitarian appeals were well under half funded in 2025 after the US cuts (Mercy Corps' own US funding fell 26%, note 12), so another agency would rarely have filled the gap. 70% (45-90%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, relief
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps pays its partners (subgrants are $96.4M of relief's $138.1M) and the money of the consortia it leads passes through its books; local partners' and volunteers' own time is the rest. 90% (75-100%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, recovery
rows.explainer: The invested share and its return come from cash trials in calmer places; recurring crises destroy assets. 0.8 (0.6-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, recovery
rows.explainer: As for relief: recovery money was cut first in 2025. 70% (45-90%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, recovery
rows.explainer: Recovery also runs through local partners and consortia whose money passes through Mercy Corps' books (subgrants are $12.0M of the line's $30.7M, p. 9); farmers' own labour and the communities' time on repairs are the rest. 90% (75-100%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, livelihoods
rows.explainer: Self-selection of participants and Mercy Corps' own uncontrolled reporting; the gains are already set near the low end of the trials. 0.75 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, livelihoods
rows.explainer: Some participants would have found the same markets, loans or advice without the programme. 85% (60-100%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, livelihoods
rows.explainer: Market-systems programmes work through firms, banks and governments that put in their own money and staff (co-investment is the design). Mercy Corps' share of the resources: 70% (50-90%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, peace
rows.explainer: One trial of a similar campaign and one null trial of Mercy Corps' own; violence data in these places are poor. 0.6 (0.3-0.9).

rows.label: Counterfactual, peace
rows.explainer: Whether the violence averted would have been averted anyway: few other organisations mediate between farmers and herders or support land commissions in these communities, but local leaders and governments do some of it on their own, and some conflicts die down by themselves. 90% (70-100%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, peace
rows.explainer: Local authorities, traditional leaders and community members give their time; governments run the courts and land commissions. 70% (40-90%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education
rows.explainer: Learning gains from other programmes' evaluations (Evans & Yuan 2022: small trials find several times the effect of large ones), earnings from wage studies; no evaluation of Mercy Corps' own schooling work. 0.6 (0.3-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, education
rows.explainer: Some young people would have stayed in school anyway. 85% (60-100%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, education
rows.explainer: Governments pay teachers in many of the schools supported. 80% (60-100%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, water
rows.explainer: The reduction is already a judgment on community sources from the meta-analyses; external validity to Mercy Corps' repaired and emergency-area systems: 0.75 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, water
rows.explainer: Some communities would have got water from the government, the utility or another agency within a few years. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, water
rows.explainer: Communities give labour and pay for repairs; utilities and local governments run some schemes. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, nutrition
rows.explainer: The share of deaths averted is a judgment from trials elsewhere (community packages delivered fully, Lassi & Bhutta 2015). 0.6 (0.3-0.9).

rows.label: Counterfactual, nutrition
rows.explainer: Ministries and UNICEF would have reached some children anyway. 70% (50-90%).

rows.label: Mercy Corps' share of the resources, nutrition
rows.explainer: Ministry of Health staff and clinics, UNICEF's therapeutic food and volunteers carry much of the work (Mercy Corps works 'in partnership with Sudan's Ministry of Health', Mercy Corps Europe's report p. 21). 50% (30-80%).

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Every count is Mercy Corps' own or a judgment from its spending: aid diverted in conflict zones, double-counted people, programmes cut short by the 2025 US stop-work orders (Mercy Corps cut its workforce by about 30%, note 17). Its accounts are audited by Grant Thornton. 85% (70-95%), for every branch.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Individual and corporate gifts are 8% of Mercy Corps' revenue ($44.7M of contributions and $3.3M of bequests against $601.5M, p. 7); unrestricted money keeps programmes open between grants and was what kept it going after the US cuts (note 17), so it neither frees others' money nor draws much in. 1 (0.9-1.05).

rows.label: Years between a gift and its spending
rows.explainer: Unrestricted gifts are spent within the year: Mercy Corps' unrestricted cash for support costs was forecast to run low by December 2026 (note 17). Its $297M of deferred revenue is institutional grants paid in advance, not donations. Judgment 0.2 years (0.05-0.5).

rows.label: Years from spending to the benefit
rows.explainer: The shared figure for relief and development work (@relief_development.delay_years_multisector, 0.3 years, 0.1-0.8): Mercy Corps' cash and water reach people in weeks; livelihood, peace and schooling work takes months to start paying.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefit
rows.explainer: The waits, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured, relief
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): Mercy Corps counts people reached but publishes no controlled measure of what its spending achieved, and the effect here is a judgment from research on this kind of work, so this branch is thin.

rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): Mercy Corps counts people reached but publishes no controlled measure of what its spending achieved, and the effect here is a judgment from research on this kind of work, so this branch is thin.

rows.label: Side effect: cash spent in local markets raises traders' and farmers' incomes
rows.explainer: Cash transfers in Kenyan villages raised non-recipients' incomes too (Egger et al. 2022, a local multiplier of about 2.5); in crisis markets with broken supply less so, and only the relief and recovery part is cash. +2% (0 to +6%) of the result.

rows.label: Side effect: cash in thin crisis markets raises prices for people not reached
rows.explainer: Where few goods get through (Gaza, besieged Sudanese towns) cash can push up prices for others; Mercy Corps runs market assessments before cash. -1% (-3% to 0).

rows.label: Side effect: aid diverted to or taxed by armed groups
rows.explainer: Aid in conflict zones is sometimes taxed at checkpoints or diverted, which can fund the violence it responds to; beyond the share lost (in the delivery adjustment) this is a harm. -1% (-4% to 0).

rows.label: Side effect: protection, psychosocial support and dignity not valued above
rows.explainer: Psychosocial sessions in Ukraine, safe spaces and the choice cash gives over in-kind aid; not in consumption or deaths. +1% (0 to +3%).

rows.label: Side effect: women's say in household decisions and coping with shocks
rows.explainer: Savings-group and women's business programmes raise women's say in household decisions and their ability to cope with shocks (Karlan et al. 2017 found women's empowerment gains), not valued in consumption: +1% (0 to +3%).

rows.label: Side effect: Mercy Corps' research and evidence used by other agencies
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps publishes evaluations and research on cash, resilience and conflict (its own trials in Afghanistan and Somalia) that other agencies and donors use in designing programmes; the money it shifts is unknown and small next to its own spending. +0.5% (0 to +2%).

rows.label: Side effect: social-enterprise investments' own results
rows.explainer: Mercy Corps' investments in social enterprises ($7.6M of programme-related investments, p. 6) sit on the balance sheet, not in the programme expenses modelled; any good they do beyond their programme use adds at most a little. 0 (0 to +1%).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.formula: ue_local_market_share + ue_price_rise_share + ue_diversion_share + ue_protection_share + ue_empowerment_share + ue_research_influence_share + ue_ventures_share
rows.explainer: The sum of the signed side effects above.
